name: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
title: Routing Across Automated Market Makers
answer: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of splitting or sequencing a trade across several on chain liquidity pools rather than sending it to one. It sits inside decentralised finance, where automated market makers price assets with a bonding curve and no order book. The topic covers the choice of venues, the order in which they are hit, and the size sent to each, all aimed at a better net execution than a single pool would give. It applies to swaps, liquidations, arbitrage and treasury conversions on public blockchains.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Routing across automated market makers is the practice of splitting or sequencing a trade across several on chain liquidity pools rather than sending it to one. It sits inside decentralised finance, where automated market makers price assets with a bonding curve and no order book. The topic covers the choice of venues, the order in which they are hit, and the size sent to each, all aimed at a better net execution than a single pool would give. It applies to swaps, liquidations, arbitrage and treasury conversions on public blockchains.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on blockchain nodes and indexers that read pool reserves, tick data and fee tiers, plus mempool access for pending transactions. Routers are usually smart contracts, sometimes paired with off chain solvers or keepers that compute the split and submit it. Common venues include constant product pools and concentrated liquidity pools, and the router must account for each venue's fee and price impact. Gas cost, block time and the risk of a transaction landing in a different state than expected all shape the design.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A router models each pool's curve, estimates output for a candidate split, and searches over allocations until the marginal price across venues is roughly equal. Simple versions compare two or three pools directly, while larger systems use graph search, convex optimisation or simulation against recent state. Slippage tolerance and a deadline bound the trade, and the contract reverts if the realised output falls short. Because state changes between quote and execution, many routers quote, simulate and then submit in one flow.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Routers hold no user funds beyond the swap in flight, but they do carry approval risk, contract risk and the risk that a pool is manipulated or illiquid. Users typically grant token allowances to the router contract, so the scope and revocability of those approvals matter. Provenance is traceable on chain, which lets anyone reconstruct the path, the pools used and the fees paid. Operators also weigh MEV exposure, since a visible route can be front run or sandwiched, and some jurisdictions treat routing activity as regulated dealing or money transmission.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Routing is moving toward intent based systems, where a user states an outcome and competing solvers find the path, and toward batch auctions that reduce MEV. Cross chain routing and unified liquidity layers are extending the same problem across bridges and rollups. Better simulation and private order flow are likely to shrink slippage further, while regulatory attention to front running and market manipulation grows. The open question is how much of the search stays on chain versus in off chain competition among solvers.
